summary: **Field Shift** is a climate-informed agricultural decision-support concept designed to help farmers make more resilient crop-rotation decisions using NASA Earth observation data. The project focuses on rainfed agricultural areas in Andalusia, Spain, where changing rainfall patterns, increasing temperatures and soil conditions can significantly influence agricultural productivity. Field Shift aims to connect climate conditions with soil moisture, vegetation health and land characteristics to provide a clearer understanding of environmental risks affecting farmland. By combining NASA POWER climate data with satellite-derived vegetation indicators and geospatial soil information, the proposed solution will help compare crop-rotation scenarios based on water requirements, soil protection, nitrogen management and economic considerations. The project's objective is to make complex environmental information more accessible and useful for farmers and agricultural advisors, supporting informed decisions, sustainable land management and long-term agricultural resilience.
details:
What does Field Shift do?

Field Shift is designed as a decision-support solution that connects environmental data with practical agricultural planning. Its main purpose is to help farmers understand how climate variability and soil characteristics influence crop performance and which crop rotations may offer greater resilience under different environmental conditions.

The proposed workflow follows a simple relationship:

Climate → Soil Water → Vegetation Stress → Soil Conditions → Crop Rotation Decisions.

The system is intended to transform these environmental indicators into understandable information that can support comparisons between alternative crop-rotation strategies.

Data and methodology

The project focuses on four agricultural areas in Andalusia: Écija, Guadix, Jerez and Úbeda.

The exploratory data analysis uses NASA POWER climate data, covering January 1981 to October 2026. The notebook examines temperature patterns through monthly time series, 12-month rolling averages and temperature extremes. It also loads additional monthly indicators, including precipitation, rainy days, humidity, wind and estimated soil moisture.

The broader technical framework identifies several complementary Earth observation datasets:

  • NASA POWER: Historical climate conditions, rainfall and temperature variability.
  • MODIS NDVI: Vegetation greenness and seasonal crop development.
  • SMAP: Surface soil-moisture conditions and drought signals.
  • SRTM: Elevation and terrain slope.
  • SoilGrids: Soil texture, organic carbon, pH and other soil characteristics.

Each dataset contributes a different perspective on agricultural conditions. Their spatial resolution, temporal coverage and data-quality limitations must be considered when interpreting results.

Decision-support approach

The proposed next stage is to develop a transparent multi-criteria scoring system that compares three alternative crop rotations.

Rotations would be assessed according to water requirements, erosion protection, soil organic matter, nitrogen management and potential income. Farmers would be able to assign different priorities to these objectives.

The system could also explore climate scenarios, such as a 20% reduction in rainfall or a 2°C increase in temperature, to examine how rotation rankings change under more challenging conditions.

Importantly, the project does not claim to have a trained model capable of predicting the objectively best crop rotation. The proposed approach uses transparent indicators and decision criteria, with agricultural assumptions subject to expert review.

Business potential and intended impact

Field Shift has the potential to develop into a digital agricultural advisory service for farmers, agricultural cooperatives and agronomists.

Its value proposition is to make Earth observation data easier to interpret and translate into practical decisions. Potential benefits include more informed crop selection, improved soil protection, more efficient water management and greater resilience to climate variability.

Possible future business models include farm-level advisory reports, subscription-based access for agricultural professionals and partnerships with farming cooperatives.

The long-term vision is to support a transition towards more sustainable and climate-adaptive agricultural practices.

Tools and technologies

The exploratory analysis uses Python, Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly and Scikit-learn. The analysis is conducted in Jupyter Notebook.

NASA POWER is the principal climate-data source used in the submitted EDA. The additional geospatial datasets form part of the proposed wider methodology.

Current development status

The current implementation establishes the climate-data analysis foundation. The integration of all proposed satellite datasets, the complete rotation-scoring engine and field validation remain future development stages.

Field Shift is intended to complement farmers' experience and professional agronomic advice, not replace it.
